content: 1. Individual interventions should include mediumto long-term follow-up to evaluate the sustainability of their effects. 2. There is a need for an increase in high-quality studies that utilize validated work-related outcomes to assess the effects of individual interventions, including those with longer follow-up durations (e.g., psychosocial intervention methods). 3. More studies are required to examine individual interventions that address suicidal behaviors and substance use outcomes. 4. The use of cluster randomized controlled trial designs should be expanded in this field, particularly for individual interventions, with follow-up durations extended to at least 12 months. 5. Outcomes that demonstrate the benefits of interventions, such as the time taken to return to work, the duration from partial to full return to work, productivity, and work ability, should be included more frequently, rather than focusing solely on reductions in absence days due to mental health conditions. 6. There is a need for more studies investigating the cost-effectiveness of intervention options aimed at facilitating return to work following absences caused by mental health conditions. 7. High-quality research is needed to determine the most effective and feasible combinations of work-directed and clinical interventions. Research Gaps for Employment of Individuals with Mental Health Conditions 8. More studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of recovery-oriented strategies that promote vocational and economic inclusion, consistently including recovery outcomes for mental health conditions and work-related outcomes relevant to employers. 9. High-quality studies should investigate the cost-effectiveness of recovery-oriented strategies that enhance vocational and economic inclusion. 10. Research should focus on the effectiveness and feasibility of implementing recovery-oriented strategies for individuals with mild to moderate mental health conditions. Research Gaps for Workplace Screening Programs 11. High-quality and adequately powered research is required to evaluate the benefits and harms of workplace screening programs and their efficacy in reducing symptoms of mental health conditions. Dissemination and Update of Guidelines 12. The guidelines are available on the WHO website in English, with the executive summary provided in all six United Nations languages. 13. National ministries responsible for mental health and occupational health will be informed of the guidelines through WHO’s regional and country offices. 14. Ministries of labor and employment, as well as representative bodies for workers and employers, will be notified via the International Labour Organization (ILO). 15. The guidelines will be shared with a broad network of international partners, including organizations committed to worker health, safety, and well-being, WHO collaborating centers, universities, NGOs, and UN agencies. Implementation 16. A policy brief, jointly developed by WHO and ILO, will accompany the guidelines to facilitate implementation. This brief will be available in six UN languages and will outline policy and implementation options derived from the guidelines. 17. WHO regional and country offices will encourage implementation at the national level. 18. Local adoption and implementation may be supported through the WHO Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan (2013–2030) and the WHO global strategy for health, environment, and climate change, both adopted by the World Health Assembly. 19. WHO will disseminate the guidelines and policy brief through its international network, including national health ministries, WHO collaborating centers, universities, NGOs, and UN agencies. 20. The ILO will promote the policy brief among its tripartite constituents, including labor ministries, employer organizations, and worker organizations, providing policy guidance on roles and responsibilities in promoting mental health at work. Monitoring and Evaluation 21. WHO will monitor the uptake and implementation of the guidelines in national policies and programs by reviewing the number of countries that have adapted or endorsed the guidelines. 22. WHO will collect regular feedback from implementation activities and key stakeholders to evaluate the usefulness and impact of the guidelines. Future Updates 23. The guidelines are expected to remain valid for five years. 24. WHO will monitor research developments in mental health promotion, prevention, and interventions for workers, particularly in areas where evidence certainty is low or very low. 25. If new evidence or considerations arise that may impact the recommendations, WHO will coordinate an update of the guidelines following the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development.
